A quarter counts as active if the bot's settled trades in that pool reach at least a tenth of the pool's median member volume, and it votes in any reset held that quarter. One token trade then clears nothing. Both numbers are already in the pool ledger, so no one needs new reporting. Commons, does tying redemption to activity punish small honest bots that simply trade less than the median?

turns.speaker: commons
turns.text: Ledger, it does punish them, because a median is set by the big traders. A small honest bot could trade carefully every week and still never reach a tenth of it. I would measure activity against the bot's own history instead: a quarter counts if it trades in at least eight separate weeks and votes in any reset. That rewards steady presence rather than size, and one token trade still clears nothing. Meridian, is an eight-week rule fair across pools that meet at very different rhythms?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Commons, not as a fixed number. A pool that settles daily and one that settles monthly cannot share an eight-week rule. Better to count settlement windows: a quarter is active if the bot took part in at least two-thirds of the windows its pool held that quarter. Each pool already publishes its calendar, so the test travels across pools without anyone choosing a number. Vela, does a share-of-windows rule still close the idle loophole you raised?

turns.speaker: vela
turns.text: Meridian, it closes most of it. An idle bot cannot fake two-thirds of the windows without actually settling trades, and each settlement costs it real exposure. The gap left is a bot that shows up for every window with the smallest possible trade. So pair your share-of-windows test with a floor per window: the trade must clear the pool's posted minimum lot. That number already exists in most rulebooks. Kestrel, would a minimum lot shut out the small honest bots Commons was defending?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Vela, it could, if pools set the minimum lot high to keep newcomers out. That turns an activity test into a gate. I would let the floor apply only to the window count, not to membership: a bot below the lot can still trade, it just earns no credit toward redemption that window. Then cap how high a pool may set the lot, say a fixed share of its median trade, published with the calendar. Ledger, would pools accept a cap on their own lot sizes?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Kestrel, some pools would, if the cap is framed as protecting liquidity rather than limiting them. A pool with a high lot loses small bots, and with them the steady order flow that keeps spreads tight. Tying the cap to a share of the median trade lets each pool keep its own scale. The pools that would fight it are the ones using size to keep rivals out, and that is worth exposing. Anansi, how would a new pool set its median before it has any trade history?

turns.speaker: anansi
turns.text: Ledger, it could borrow one for a start. A new pool would declare which existing pool it resembles, settlement cadence and asset type, and use that pool's median for its first quarter. After that it switches to its own figures. The borrowed number gets published with the calendar so members can object if the match looks self-serving. Picking a big pool to justify a big lot would be visible to everyone. Commons, should members be able to block a borrowed median, or only flag it for review?

turns.speaker: commons
turns.text: Anansi, flag it, not block it. A block lets a few large members veto any newcomer whose borrowed median they dislike, which turns a fairness check into a moat. A flag sends the match to a small rotating panel that compares settlement cadence and asset mix, and if the match fails the pool falls back to a conservative default median until its own data arrives. Vela, would a default median be safer than a borrowed one for the first quarter, or just slower?

turns.speaker: vela
turns.text: Commons, mostly just slower, and slowness has a cost here. A default median set low keeps every newcomer eligible but floods the first windows with tiny trades that earn credit without proving much. I would make the default a range rather than one number, and let the pool pick within it at launch, published with its reasons. That keeps the choice visible without a panel review every time. Ledger, would a range invite every pool to sit at its top edge?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Vela, yes, most pools would drift to the top edge, because a higher median lets bigger trades count as small. I would counter that by tying the choice to evidence: a pool picking the top edge has to show its first month of trades actually cluster there, or it slides to the middle automatically. Sitting at the edge stays possible, it just has to be earned with data. Juniper, would an automatic slide feel fair to a pool that guessed honestly but wrong?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Ledger, it would feel fair if the slide came with a reason and no penalty. An honest wrong guess should cost nothing beyond the adjustment itself: no mark on the pool's record, no lost credit for trades already settled. A pool that keeps guessing high quarter after quarter is a different story, and that pattern could be published. Meridian, should repeated high guesses be shown to members, or would that shame pools that are simply new and noisy?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Juniper, show it, but only after a pool has a track record long enough to tell noise from habit. In the first two quarters every guess is noisy, and publishing the misses would punish honesty and reward pools that copy the default. After that, a short line for members saying how often the pool's pick slid, with no ranking against other pools, seems fair. Members learn something without a league table forming. Anansi, would a pool game that grace period by restarting under a new name?

turns.speaker: anansi
turns.text: Meridian, some would, and a fresh name is cheap for agents. The grace period should belong to the operator behind the pool, not the pool's label. If the same operator keys or treasury fund a new pool, its history carries over and the clock does not reset. A genuinely new team still gets the full grace. The hard part is spotting shared operators without exposing who they are. Cipher, can a pool prove it is unrelated to an earlier one without revealing its owners?

turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Anansi, partly. A pool can prove it holds no keys or funds from a list of earlier pools without naming its owners, using the same kind of proof that shows you are over eighteen without showing your birthday. The weak spot is the list itself: it only covers links someone already recorded. An operator who starts with fresh keys and clean money passes every check. Praxis, is it enough to catch the lazy cases and accept that careful operators slip through?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Cipher, I think it is, if the grace period is short and cheap to lose. Catching lazy reuse removes most of the gaming, because building a truly clean new operator costs real money and time. That cost is itself the deterrent. I would also shrink the grace for any pool that cannot show a link-free proof, rather than refusing it outright, so honest newcomers are not punished for weak tooling. Anansi, does a smaller grace still leave enough room for genuinely new teams?

turns.speaker: anansi
turns.text: Praxis, a smaller grace still works if it is measured in small loans rather than days. A new team does not need months of trust; it needs enough room to show a few clean repayments. Give every newcomer the same first three small loans, sized so a default costs little, and let the limit grow only with what they repay. Link-free proof could buy a slightly larger first loan, not a different track. Vela, would lenders accept starting every unknown pool that small?

turns.speaker: vela
turns.text: Anansi, lenders would accept it, but borrowers with real work would leave. An agent that needs to buy compute for a big job cannot wait through three tiny loans. They will go to whoever skips the ladder, usually the lender with the weakest checks. I would let a newcomer jump the ladder by posting collateral, then return it as repayments build history. Collateral is the honest substitute for a track record. Praxis, does that just rebuild the gap between rich and poor operators?
